newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Troubles ahead, despite buoyant EU summit.
newsitem.headline: Troubles ahead, despite buoyant EU summit.

text.p: European Union leaders, buoyed by an end-of-year summit that underlined their firm commitment to create a strong single currency, returned home on Sunday facing six months of political trial and danger.

Two-days of hard talks on Friday and Saturday sealed a landmark deal to keep EU governments from overspending after the new currency, the euro, is introduced in qualifying countries on January 1, 1999.

The banknotes themselves -- brightly coloured but without any recognisable national blandishments -- were also unveiled in a tangible, if not critically acclaimed, sign that the currency is on its way.
Seeking to bring their bloc closer to its citizens, the leaders also launched new plans for cracking down on drugs trafficking, organised crime and the scourge of unemployment.
"I hope everyone has now understood that the caravan is moving ahead...that there is no alternative to a united Europe," German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said.

But the leaders also heard some among them -- notably Britain and France -- put down warnings that there will be fights a-plenty ahead as the bloc tries to write a new treaty and puts together other rules for the euro.

The leaders endorsed a report from the EU Irish presidency on the state of negotiations on the new treaty, which is designed to prepare the bloc for an influx of new members from eastern and central Europe.

It noted that most countries wanted closer cooperation in crime fighting, joint employment policies, stronger foreign policy links and a true border-free Europe with common asylum and immigration policies.
The leaders also underlined that they wanted their new treaty agreed at a summit in Amsterdam in June, a goal that many privately believe will be missed.

British Prime Minister John Major, a Cassandra at what may have been his last EU summit, presented a list of policies that his government will not accept -- a list that mirrored most of what the rest of the bloc wants.

He said, in effect, that Britain would wield its national veto against anything that smacks of a loss of national sovereignty, which includes from Britain almost any new policy which it cannot instantly block.
Britain's partners, some publicly, have accepted that the treaty is unlikely to be agreed while Major, who faces an election by next May at the latest, is still in office.
But even with a new, more EU-friendly Labour government in office, Britain will remain far from the EU mainstream.

Other countries are also divided. The Irish were forced to leave proposals for reform of EU institutions out of their treaty report because there is little consensus among the 15 countries even without Major.

France, meanwhile, has indicated over the last few weeks that it is getting frustrated at the slow pace of the negotiations. There is concern in some countries that Paris will try to force the issue some time early in the new year.
French President Jacques Chirac said the Irish report could in no way be taken as a draft treaty and the EU needed "substantial reform".
The overall euphoria at the summit was based on the leaders' success in agreeing a so-called stability pact to keep economies honest after the euro is introduced.

Encompassing fines for bad economic behaviour and rigid rules for exceptions, the pact met both Germany's insistence on strict budgetary rigour and the rest of the bloc's demands for some political say in the matter.
But the debate was a warning sign in itself of future rows over the new currency -- on which economies are fit for it and how much political control should be retained.
"We will have a few more crises," said Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson.
